newsitem.title: USA: NYS monitor says bigger rev forecast can be met.
newsitem.headline: NYS monitor says bigger rev forecast can be met.

text.p: The New York State Comptroller on Friday said that while Gov. George Pataki and the legislature failed to agree on how much extra revenues the state will get, a $1.3 billion estimate can be met.

The Republican governor, the Senate -- which is led by Republicans -- and the Democrat-controlled Assembly all have produced different estimates of how much extra funds the state will get during fiscal 1997 and 1998.
While they failed to meet a March 10 deadline for producing a consensus forecast, they narrowed their differences for this period to $1.3 billion from $1.6 billion, the comptroller said.

The $1.3 billion estimate is double the amount forecast by Pataki, who has estimated that the state will get an extra $650 million from late February until the end of the 1998 fiscal year, largely because Wall Street banks and brokerage houses are expected to keep earning big profits.
The Assembly had predicted a $2 billion windfall, and the more conservative Senate had looked for revenues to surge $922 million over the initial estimates.

In a prepared statement, H. Carl McCall's office said: "McCall's report noted the upper forecast is achievable but is associated with a higher level of risk." The findings by H. Carl McCall were contained in his annual report on revenue estimates, which also noted that while Wall Street's profits have rallied, the state's overall job growth has been weak.

Cautioning that the governor and the legislature still remain far apart in their various estimates, McCall, who is a potential Democratic challenger for the governship, warned against using inflated revenue projections to boost expenditures. "The biggest danger lies in how they decide to spend the money. Basing a spending plan on higher revenue estimates will make it difficult to close any budget gap that could occur with an economic downturn," he said.
